text: The Concept of Resistance in Self Psychology CRAYTON E. ROWE, JR., M.S.W., B.C.D.* Self psychology views resistances as protecting a vulnerable self Resistances are seen as efforts to maintain levels of organization that patients have achieved within the context of their traumatic life situation. Patients feel able to move forward in the treatment when the importance of their need to maintain their developmental position is understood. This view is in contrast to the traditional view of resistances as treatment interferences that must be overcome as they defend against awareness of impulses and allow for unconscious instinctual gratification. Freud^ first mentioned the clinical fact of resistance in his work with Elisabeth von R. in 1892. At that time Freud developed a technique whereby he attempted to elicit ideas from the patient through pressing the patient's head. He took note that Elisabeth von R. often revealed information only after he pressed her head three times even though she knew her thoughts after the first time. It was Freud's difficulty with this particular patient that led him to his clinical concept of resistance: "In the course of this difficult work I began to attach a deeper significance to the resistance offered by the patient in the reproduction of her memories and to make a careful collection of the occasions on which it was particularly marked" (p. 154). Freud's understanding of resistance inspired him to his conceptualization of defense and his shift in technique from deliberate suggestions to free associations. It was his understanding >6f resistance that also prompted his conceptualization of the structural theory and led to the development of traditional psychoanalysis as we know it today. TRADITIONAL VIEW OF RESISTANCE—DEFENSE AGAINST AWARENESS AND RESOLUTION OF CONFLICT ^'^ concept of resistance as a defense against awareness that requires "overcoming" to effect changes, is the traditional view of resistance "Past chair, the National Membership Committee on Psychoanalysis in Clinical Social Work; Distinguished Practitioner of Social Work, the National Academies of Practice; founding member. The New York Institute for Psychoanalytic Self Psychology; training analyst. The New York Freudian Society and the National Psychological Association for Psychoanalysis. Mailing address: 230 West End Avenue, Suite ID, New York, NY 10023-3662. AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY, Vol. 50, No. 1, Winter 1996 66 The Concept of Resistance in Self Psychology held today. Most analytic writing, including those of the British object- relations school, subscribe to this traditional view generally understood as providing protection against awareness of impulse and drive derivatives'* and as interfering with the resolving of intrapsychic conflict. Resistances allow patients to seek unconscious instinctual satisfaction and safeguard them against painful afTects that accompany conscious awareness. Dewald' fuUy captures this traditional view. H e considers that resistances have both a strategic and tactical level of organization: Strategic resistances would be those basic unconscious core psychic operations through which the patient continues to seek satisfaction of infantile and early childhood drives and drive derivatives, object choices, or adaptive and defensive psychic operations. . . The tactical resistances represent superimposed individual intrapsychic and interpersonal behavior patterns in various hierarchies of organi- zation by which patients defend themselves against conscious awareness of strategic core resistances and the conflicts with which they are interlocked (pp. 61-62). Dewald is clear that resistances operate against the purposes of analysis: In a general sense, the handling of resistances (both tactical and strategic) involves the establishment and maintenance of a therapeutic situation in which the patient increasingly accepts and uses the analyst's vantage point in regard to change and psychic maturation, and increasingly recognizes his own resistances as internal psychic operations activated in opposition to the avowed purpose of the analysis (p. 63). SELF PSYCHOLOGY'S VIEW OF RESISTANCE—PROTECTING THE SELF In contrast to the traditional view of resistances as interferences and obstacles that must be removed or modified, self psychology recognizes that resistances are important in preserving the self. Kohut^ succinctly made this point: "All these so-called resistances serve the basic ends of the self; they never have to be 'overcome' " (p. 148). Kohut^ thought that the traditional view of gaining access to the unconscious through overcoming resistances, could explain delimited units of psychic function such as slips of tongue and other psychopathology of everyday life. The traditional view could also explain symptoms of the transference neuroses and a majority of dreams. However, Kohut thought the traditional view fell short in elucidating personality in general and personality disturbances in particular. Before one can understand how resistances serve the needs of the self, one must have an understanding of Kohut's fundamental contributions of selfobject and selfobject transferences—concepts which form the nucleus of self psychology theory. 67 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY KOHUT'S CONTRIBUTIONS OF SELFOBJECT AND SELFOBJECT TRANSFERENCES Selfobject needs and selfobject transferences are among Kohut's most fundamental discoveries born out of an attunement to the patient's experi- Kohut was able to suspend his theoretical convictions and perceive data more clearly from patients' experience. As a result he was able to discover his patients' needs for mirroring, and come to his conceptualization of selfobject as an impersonal experience of a function that is provided. Self psychology's focus on selfobject as the experience of a function provided is clearly different from that of object relations theory where the focus is on the object per se and not on the functions provided by the object. The differences in these concepts are not always clearly understood. '^ Kohut's discovery of his concept of selfobject was poignantly described in his work with Miss F.: "Thus I refused to entertain the possibility that I was not an object for the patient, not an amalgam with the patient's childhood loves and hatreds, but only, as I reluctantly came to see, an impersonal function, without significance except insofar as it related to the kingdom of her own remobilized narcissistic grandeur and exhibitionism"'^ (p. 288). Kohut's^"* definition of selfobject as the experience of the funcdons provided was further clarified in a 1980 letter to a colleague: "Whether cognitively insufficiently separated from the self, as may be the case in infancy and in certain archaic merger states later in life, or, as is most often the case, in particular in the older child and in the adult, cognitively separated from it, the selfobject is defined by our experience of its function" (p. 671). Kohut^ returned to his definition of selfobject as the experience of functions provided in his 1984 posthumously published work. How Does Analysis Cure? Here he considered the general meaning of selfobject to be ". . .that dimension of our experience of another person that relates to the person's functions in shoring up our self. . ." and the specific meaning as relating to the earliest developmental experiences that are carried forward and into the present (p. 49). Self psychology sees transferences as mobilizations of unrequited selfob- ject needs for idealizing; for recognition of exhibitionistic expressions of ideas, talents, and abilities; and for experiencing alikeness with others. These needs emerge as strivings toward establishing self-cohesion and continue to unfold and develop in the treatment as mature forms of selfobject transfer- ences. Kohut emphasized that through the development of the selfobject 68 The Concept of Resistance in Self Psychology transferences, the patient's arrested development can be set in motion and come to completion.^'^' In his concluding remarks in How Does Analysis Cure?, Kohut^ reminded us that the analysis of tbe transferences was the core of psychoanalytic attention: "Self psychology does not advocate a change in the essence of analytic technique. The transferences are allowed to unfold and their analysis—the understanding of the transference reactions, their explanation in dynamic and genetic terms—occupies, now as before, the center of the analyst's attention" (p. 208). As the selfobject transferences unfold, the analyst must be able to differentiate their various forms in order to understand the specific develop- mental needs of the patient: "The ability to differentiate between various types of selfobject transferences also gives us the opportunity to study in greater detail the developmental line characteristically associated witb the archaic form of a particular self-selfobject relationship—from the archaic state tbat is revived at the beginning of the transference to the mature state which, as a result of tbe systematic and patiently pursued working-through process, may be attained at the end of successful analyses"^ (p. 202). It is important to note tbat self psychology does not advocate a change in tbe essence of psychoanalytic technique in that the transferences are tbe focus of treatment. However, as stated above, the conceptualization of transference differs from traditional understanding. In self psychology, the patient's selfobject needs are seen as developing into mature forms of selfobject transferences. This development is a growth experience for tbe patient and is contradistinction to tbe generally understood traditional meaning of transference as resistance to awareness.^ Self psychology recognizes that resistances to experiencing selfobject needs are activated if tbese needs threaten tbe patient with repeating potentially destabilizing experiences.'^ To oversimplify for a moment, pa- tients wbo have been seriously disillusioned as children will resist emerging needs to idealize for fear of further disillusionment. Patients who have suffered humiliation will resist sharing unique thoughts and ideas that could be tbe target of criticism. Therefore, one can say that there are resistances to the development of the selfobject transferences as tbe patient attempts to protect against repeating traumatic experiences. Severely traumatized pa- tients with serious defects in the structure of the self, can become fixated on arcbaic defensive selfobject configurations. Patients retum to tbese protec- tive patterns of experiencing during the working-through process and as new forms of selfobject transferences develop. However, this is in contrast to tbe traditional view of the compulsion to repeat which is the repeating of 69 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY patterns of behavior that provide instinctual pleasure or, to use Freud's term, "unpleasure,"^^ as an effort to master and bind excitation. EXAMPLES OF RESISTANCES The following brief case examples of Ms. O. and Mr. V., taken from their complete analysis which I previously reported, '^ highlight the self-preserva- tive function of primitive idealizations that were understood as discrete and necessary ways of organizing severe psychological traumata into elaborate selfobject configurations. The patients' efforts to maintain their idealizations were seen as necessary resistances to preserve the self and not as resistances to awareness as in the traditional sense. Understanding the self-preservative importance of these selfobject con- figurations facilitated the intemalization and structure-building process that in turn allowed the patient's heretofore thwarted selfobject needs to emerge and develop as selfobject transferences. Case of Mr. V. Mr. V., a thirty-two-year-old intelligent, highly anxious and somber man, was adopted at birth. At three years of age his adopted parents died, and he was sent to a series of foster homes where he was sexually abused and suffered innumerable traumatic separations. At seventeen years of age he left the last home and fended for himself. He would frequently solicit both female and male prostitutes who would agree to abuse and humiliate him. Mr. V. had been a successful computer salesman but had lost the job. He had recently gone through a divorce and moved in with a cousin and planned to stay until he found work. He angrily stated that he came to treatment because his cousin insisted that he get help as he was not finding work and not making efforts to move. He expected people to misunderstand him and "rip him off." He was sure that I, like everyone else, only wanted his money. As treatment progressed, I came to see Mr. V. as being fixated on primitive idealizations. His idealistic and perfectionistic views left him disillusioned and enraged at the realities of everyday living. He easily became angry with friends and would not speak with them for long periods. A major theme of his fantasies consisted of an elaborate primitive idealized world of friendly animals who lived in a magical forest. It was a world where there was peacefulness and beautiful colors. Mr. V. would spend considerable time during the day thinking about and visualizing his imaginary world. I learned that Mr. V.'s forest world of friendly animals and beautiful colors had developed in his childhood and protected him against the relentless traumata he faced daily. Mr. V. vividly explained: "I don't 70 The Concept of Resistance in Self Psychology remember anybody really giving a damn when I was growing up. , .maybe you're the only one, . .1 don't think I can open my eyes—so sleepy. I see these beautiful colors. . .1 know about yoga meditation. If I close my eyes, I can sometimes keep the beautiful blue color for a little while. My mother is in here somewhere. . .maybe I trusted her. I don't mean my real mother, I think I was adopted at birth but they [adopted parents] died when I was around 3. Then foster homes. . .don't know how many, . .1 guess that's what happens." Mr. V. began to breathe heavily at this point and then said: "When I give up my blue light, every time, I feel I can't take a deep breath." Mr. V. went on to say that he imagined his real mother to have been as beautiful as his blue light. He remembered as a child he cut out cardboard figures of animals and people to relieve his loneliness and withdrew more and more into his isolated world of fantasy that persisted throughout his life. My understanding that Mr. V.'s primitive idealization protected him from the effects of his relentless childhood traumata, was crucial in helping him to feel understood. For example, on one occasion I made the following intervention: "More and more you're letting me in on the pain you have endured. I understand how the "blue light" has been so important in your life." Mr. V., who was breathing uneasily, nodded in agreement. He began to relax and said: "I had the feeling of wanting to tell you more, and then I thought I couldn't. But I guess I can." For the first time Mr. V. began to describe an instance where he was sexually abused at seven years of age by a man who was an acquaintance of his foster mother. Mr. V. nervously and sorrowfully described how this man tied his legs and arms as an apparent game and then, when Mr. V. was helpless, took off his clothes and penetrated him. After lengthy working through of his seemingly unshakable expectations that people would take advantage of him and his defensive reactions to these expectations, Mr. V. became less preoccupied with his primitive world and moved forward in the treatment. He developed an idealizing selfobject transference and then a mirror transference where he was able to work through his anxieties and inhibitions around learning and making mistakes. In time, his defensive bravado diminished, and he was able to accept and find satisfaction in obtainable goals. For example, he pursued graduate studies in sociology with the goal of making changes within the social system. Mr. V, had moved from maintaining his protective idealized forest world of animals and colors to studying how realistic changes could be made to improve the social system that had been relentlessly traumatic for him. 71 AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PSYCHOTHERAPY Case of Ms. O. Ms. O., an intelligent, attractive twenty-six-year-old Hispanic woman, was the youngest of six siblings. She lived in poverty in a crowded apartment, with only two rooms, one of which served both as a bedroom and kitchen for the entire family. For the first two years of her Ufe, she had the attention of her parents, but then suffered abrupt and severe emotional estrangement from them as they became overwhelmed by their circumstances and had little time for her. Ms. O. was sexually molested by her older brother when she was five years of age and was subjected to the tiightly sounds of her mother and father having intercourse in an adjoining bed. Ms. O. wet the bed and compulsively masturbated with the fantasies of sexually submitting to a threatening male figure who was kind to her as long as she obeyed him. These symptoms only subsided when she left home and went to live with relatives at the age of thirteen. Ms. O. sought treatment as she had been suffering a number of physical symptoms such as severe chest, back, and leg pains, headaches, and throat infections. She was worried that she was not worthy of her husband and feared his leaving her for another woman. Ms. O. seemed highly motivated to begin treatment and quickly viewed me as an exalted male figure who had great intelligence and who would solve her problems and rid her of her pains. Her diminished view of herself in relation to her husband and to me was seen as she tearfully began to speak in her initial interview: "I'm glad to have someone to speak with since my husband wanted me to. He is concerned about my leg and back pains and feels there is something wrong—you know, maybe some nerve disease. . .1 can tell you understand—I am glad I have an older man. My doctor first suggested someone else—a younger man—but I didn't want a young man. I don't know why—I don't think that I could depend on a younger man. I don't think that I could trust a woman either." Ms. O. continued in a self-demeaning manner: "I don't know why I said that—I never talk about anyone. I am weak and a crybaby, not like my husband. When my husband goes on business trips, I am up the wall—the depression and emptiness are too much. I become a crazy woman—screaming and all that." As the analysis continued, it became clearer that Ms. O. had survived her relentless traumatic childhood experiences through maintaining a primitive fantasy of being a mindless servant to a powerful idealized figure whom she must obey. She felt safe as long as she was helpless and powerless. Like Mr. V., Ms. O. was fixated on a primitive, albeit qualitatively 72 The Concept of Resistance in Self Psychology different, form of idealization. (Fixations can also occur on primitive forms of grandiose selfobject configurations as a result of severe childhood trau- mata.'^ This can result in hyperactive, and grandiose behavior especially seen in disadvantaged children living in poverty environments '^"^'). Ms. O. was able to describe her experience of this primitive idealization early in the treatment: ". . .1 think I remember the hopelessness—I think I feel it right now—like I'm sinking—back into the helpless position where everyone knows more than I do. It's miserable, but like we've said, it's safe. Nobody says I'm stupid there. It's like being stupid already—like a foregone conclusion." (Ms. O.'s experience of helplessness was one of feeling dead- ened to all sensation.) As Ms. O. gained a fuller understanding of the self-preservative impor- tance of her primitive idealization, her need to experience herself in her protective diminished way subsided. Little by little she began to develop an assertiveness as a mirror transference unfolded. She became more comfort- able with her emerging grandiosity as the working through of her fears of being dominant took place. After a sequence of working through disappoint- ments that I was not all wise and at times even confused, Ms. O. developed an idealizing transference based upon a realistic appreciation of our work. Ms. O. eventually completed high school and college. She secured work as an administrator in a department store and no longer viewed her husband as being superior. SUMMARY Resistances in self psychology are seen as attempts to protect the self from a potentially destabilizing condition that can be precipitated by the revival of memories of actual experiences or fantasies of past traumatic experiences. Unlike the traditional view of resistances as defensive opera- tions that interfere with the treatment, resistances in self psychology are considered to be efforts at maintaining levels of organization which provide security to an enfeebled self. Resistances can be precipitated by the treatment process itself if the treatment situation poses a potential analogous traumatic situation for the patient. For example, patients who have suffered humiliation and embarrass- ment in expressing ideas may find it difficult to express their thoughts and find it uncomfortable to be the focus of analytic attention. Several examples serve to show how severely traumatized patients can become fixated on primitive, highly organized selfobject configurations. As patients feel understood, they internalize anxiety-relieving functions.
